doc.title: Ingrid Sertso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, August 11, 2014

title: Meditation, enlightenment, Van Gogh and Chet Baker
summary: Meditation in workshops; creative openness as enlightenment, with artists and drugs.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Life philosophy: faith, karma and how to live

blocks.x: When you’re doing a couple of days of the Creative Music workshops, do you do activities that sort of might cleanse the palette of all the sounds that everybody has been hearing, and all the interaction. Is there a point —

Oh yeah, it’s a big part of it. A big part of it is you go back to being alive, which means breathe. My voice workshop is breathe in, breathe out, inhale, exhale. It’s the only way we are in the moment. Stuff comes up in our mind, you see it, you don’t get involved, you let it go and you go back to just breathe in, breathe out. Be totally in the moment. And the moment, the second you express yourself creatively and it comes from a total open place, that’s the state of enlightenment. That would be the state of enlightenment in Buddhism. Vincent Van Gogh — I went to the museum in Holland. You faint. The energy that comes from his original pictures, the light of the colors, the sunshine he created in the pictures, I mean he was painting in France and so on, you can only do something like that when you have these glimpses of enlightenment. He totally identified with the sunflowers, with the sun. He totally identified. But then he goes back into total neurosis, cuts his ear off, drinks absinthe, which is the worst liquor you can drink. It’s anise liquor you know. The French are still drinking it. But that together with the painting in the sun can do you in. It’s an enlightened, all these big big masters and big musicians, you know, if they weren’t totally on drugs then — if you listen to Chet Baker when he was very young there is a lot of humor and vitality in it you know. Later on it became a little bit more dragging — his voice was a little bit more off tune.
